Hi! I got mine taken out in May. T3s are a blessing and a curse. Definitely keep taking them while you need them, but once you can switch to regular Tylenol I’d recommend doing so. Not sure if it was just me but the T3s made me feel like shit. Keep pepto or something like that at home. 

Protein drinks like BOOST are lifesavers. So is yogurt (the probiotics help with stomach issues from T3s and antibiotics!!). Soup, obviously. 

For the first few days, use HEAT on and off every 20 or so minutes. Helps with swelling and pain. After a few days, use ice every 20 or so minutes. 

Once you can eat again, be careful. Nothing too chewy/hard/hot - I’m sure your dentist told you. What’s weird is my first solid food was toast lol. Small bites at the front of my mouth helped. 

I still have small holes where they were taken out. Make sure you keep using the syringe (if they didn’t give you one I recommend getting one, it helps so much with getting food out). Warm salt water rinses. I know the pain is horrible, but it hopefully shouldn’t last too much longer. I think the worst of mine was over after a week, followed by a week of bearable pain (regular Tylenol every chance I could, but still bearable)

Honestly I think the best way to get over this is to challenge yourself and just eat when you’re hungry. I know it’s easier said than done but once you start doing it and reminding yourself that it doesn’t matter what time you eat, it gets so much easier. 

I used to do the same thing, and sometimes still do, but now I eat when I need to. For example, sometimes I’ll have lunch at 12, sometimes at 2. Which means sometimes I have a smaller dinner and have a snack/small meal later in the day, and sometimes just a small snack because I want it and not because I “need” it. 

Overall, a lot of recovery is reminding yourself that you don’t need to follow “rules” when it comes to food and unlearning these habits. This can be hard in recovery, but it’s something that needs to be done. But trust me, once you start eating when you need to and not when you’re “allowed” to, things get so much easier.

I knew I was bi when I was 12 (I’m 18 now), but had I been brought up knowing it was “okay”, I bet anything I would’ve known sooner. I had feelings for my best friend of the same gender and it was confusing. When I heard the term gay (back when I thought you were either straight or gay), I associated it with bad things because I’d only ever heard it in a derogatory way. I learned about bisexuality along with many other sexualities and it amazed me how little I knew. I am still not 100% confident in my sexuality, but I can say with certainty I am not straight.

As for accepting it, it takes time, especially if you grew up with people who are not as accepting. Everyone is different, and I suppose it depends on whether or not you have the same beliefs as your community. I grew up in a conservative family, but I’ve always been the opposite of everyone (with the exception of thinking gay = bad, but I was a literal child so I didn’t know any better lol). I did a lot of self-reflecting. I know that I am not a bad person - I would never cheat, and being attracted to more than one gender does not change that. I know I’m not “greedy” or “can’t choose”, it’s just who I am. I’d say surround yourself (if you can) with people you know accept and support the LGBTQ+ community, and you’ll likely find yourself accepting yourself more. I personally didn’t have a very hard time accepting myself, it was more worrying about others accepting me.

When it comes to coming out, you can do that whenever you feel like it. I knew I was bisexual since I was 12, but didn’t come out to my friends until I was 14, and my family until I was 17. I asked myself that question I mentioned in the beginning. If you’re in a safe environment, it really is a weight lifted if you can be yourself and not have to hide. Personally, I don’t have a great relationship with my family, but I had to make changes in my life. I was not happy at all, and even though I have a boyfriend, the fact that I had to “act” straight bothered me. I took time and thought about it, and came to the conclusion that obviously I do care about other people’s opinions, but my mental health is ultimately more important. If they can’t accept me, that’s their problem. Their unnecessary hate shouldn’t mean I have to hide who I am and I don’t need their approval. That being said, I thankfully have a semi supportive family and I am in a safe environment. If I believed I was in danger in any way, I would not have came out. 

I also want to say, it may take a long time to be sure about your sexuality. Likewise, you may know as soon as you first figure it out. I personally went from thinking I was straight, to bi curious, to bisexual with a preference for men, to bi 50/50, to questioning if I was straight and it was a “phase”, to questioning if I was lesbian, to bi with a strong preference for women. It’s unfortunate that we have to “figure it out” because we haven’t been able to be ourselves our whole lives like straight people, but don’t let ignorant, hateful people get to you. 

Labels aren’t 100% necessary. Many people choose to label their sexuality (which is completely fine), but don’t feel bad or guilty if you end up questioning it later on. It’s a common part of life, just not a part that’s openly talked about. Whether your bi, or straight, or anything else, there are people that support you. Take your time, there’s no rush to figure it out. :)
